pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 11–13. Radiometric dating — radioactive isotopes decay at a known rate (half-life), so the parent:daughter ratio in a sample gives an ABSOLUTE age — taught by manipulating decay and half-life until the exponential pattern and the choice of the right isotope-clock become intuitive.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS3 chemistry (atoms, elements; particle model) building toward GCSE physics radioactivity (half-life); working-scientifically with ratios and models.
• Standards — US (NGSS): HS-ESS1-6 / MS-ESS1-4 use of radiometric evidence to date rocks and organise geologic time.
• Operational details: define half-life = time for half the parent to decay to daughter; after n half-lives, parent fraction = (1/2)^n. Emphasise it is a RATIO measurement, not a countdown from a known start. Contrast clocks: carbon-14 (~5,730 yr half-life; organic; useful to ~50,000 yr) vs uranium-lead / potassium-argon (millions–billions of yr; igneous rock). Explain WHY C-14 cannot date dinosaur bones (66 My ≫ ~50 ky; effectively no C-14 left) and why we date volcanic layers around fossils.
• Checkpoint: Tier A: state that after one half-life, half the parent is left. Tier B: given a parent:daughter ratio and a half-life, work out how many half-lives / the approximate age. Tier C: explain why carbon-14 is useless for dinosaurs and which isotope system and material you'd use instead, and why.
bestPractices: Build the exponential intuition by repeated halving before introducing the (1/2)^n formula.
Frame dating as reading a RATIO of how far decay has run, not a stopwatch started at a known moment.
Contrast isotope systems by half-life and material so students learn to MATCH the clock to the age range.
Confront the dinosaur-bone case directly to fix the common carbon-14 misconception.
Clarify that we usually date igneous layers bracketing a fossil, not the fossil itself.
keyRepresentations: A decay grid of parent atoms flipping to daughter over time.
An exponential half-life decay curve marked at 50%, 25%, 12.5%.
A parent:daughter ratio bar linked to number of half-lives.
A comparison chart of isotope systems (C-14, U-Pb, K-Ar) by half-life and use.
A rock section showing dateable volcanic ash above and below a fossil layer.
commonMisconceptions: 'You can carbon-date dinosaur bones' — C-14's ~50,000-year range is far too short for 66-million-year fossils.
'Radiometric dating counts down from when the animal died like a stopwatch' — it reads the parent:daughter ratio of a decay process.
'After two half-lives everything has decayed' — a quarter of the parent remains; decay is exponential, never reaching zero cleanly.
'We date the fossil itself' — usually the surrounding volcanic rock is dated, bracketing the fossil's age.
'Half-life changes with conditions' — it is essentially constant, which is what makes it a reliable clock.

learn.summary: For ages 11–13, this concept builds understanding of radiometric dating: a radioactive parent isotope decays to a daughter with a characteristic, constant half-life, so the parent:daughter RATIO in a sample yields an absolute age. Key ideas: half-life = time for half the parent to decay; after n half-lives the parent fraction = (1/2)^n; dating reads how far decay has run, not a stopwatch from a known start; and the isotope-clock must be matched to the age range (carbon-14 ~5,730 yr half-life, organic, useful to ~50,000 yr; uranium-lead / potassium-argon for millions-to-billions of years, igneous rock). The core activity is a manipulable decay model; strong companions are a ratio/age computation task and a clock-matching question; a static annotated decay curve and a scientist dialogue address specific aspects (pattern reading and the 'why date the ash, not the bone' misconception) as supporting scaffolds.

activities.title: Wind the radioactive clock: halving and solving for age
feedback: If a learner predicts the parent is all gone after one half-life, show the grid: half remains, and after two half-lives a quarter still remains — decay is exponential and approaches but never cleanly reaches zero.
If a learner reads a 1:3 parent:daughter ratio as one half-life, point out that 1:3 means only one quarter of the parent is left, which takes two halvings.
When carbon-14 is chosen for the dinosaur bone, use the 'too little parent left to measure / out of range' result to prompt switching to a long-lived system and to a dateable igneous layer.
If a learner describes dating as 'measuring elapsed time directly', recast it as comparing the proportion of parent left to daughter formed, read against the known half-life.
activities.rationale: Half-life is a dynamic quantitative relationship; repeatedly halving a visible population before meeting the (1/2)^n formula builds the exponential intuition, and inverting the task (ratio to age) plus matching the clock to the timescale targets the core objective and the carbon-14 misconception together.
sourceClaims: Half-life is the time for half of a radioactive parent isotope to decay to its daughter product; measuring the parent:daughter ratio gives an absolute age.

Carbon-14 (half-life ~5,730 years) is useful for dating organic material up to roughly 50,000 years; older/inorganic materials require systems like uranium-lead or potassium-argon (millions to billions of years), so dinosaur bones (~66 My) cannot be carbon-dated.
learnerActions: Start with a grid of 'parent' atoms and advance a time-slider; watch atoms flip to a 'daughter' colour as a half-life counter ticks.
Before advancing, predict what fraction of parent will remain after 1, 2, and 3 half-lives, then check against the grid and a parent:daughter ratio bar.
Connect the pattern to the formula: parent fraction = (1/2)^n after n half-lives (1/2, then 1/4, then 1/8).

Switch to 'mystery sample' mode: given a measured parent:daughter ratio such as 1 part parent to 3 parts daughter, and assuming the sample started with no daughter and nothing has been added or lost since, work out how many half-lives have passed (here, two — one quarter of the parent remains) and estimate the age using the half-life.
Use a clock-picker to choose the right isotope system for a given material and age (e.g. carbon-14 for recent organic material; uranium-lead for a 100-million-year rock).

Try to carbon-date a dinosaur bone and observe the result: too little original carbon-14 left to measure, because dinosaur fossils are at least 66 million years old, far beyond carbon-14's ~50,000-year range; then switch to uranium-lead on a bracketing volcanic layer.
activities.intendedInsight: Dating is not a stopwatch started at a known moment — it reads how far a decay with a known, constant half-life has run via the parent:daughter ratio, and the clock's half-life must match the age being measured. The number of atoms decaying per unit time is not constant; it falls as the parent is depleted, because each half-life removes half of whatever parent remains.

activities.title: Compute the age and match the clock
feedback: For a sample with one quarter of its parent remaining, confirm two half-lives have passed and multiply by the half-life for the age.
If a learner selects carbon-14 for a 100-million-year rock, remind them carbon-14 is exhausted beyond ~50,000 years and a long-lived system is required.
When ordering by age, check reasoning uses the ratio consistently rather than absolute counts.
activities.rationale: A computation-and-selection task tests the mathematics and clock-choice directly; it consolidates rather than builds the decay intuition, so it works best after or alongside the manipulable model.
sourceClaims: Half-life is the time for half of a radioactive parent isotope to decay to its daughter product; measuring the parent:daughter ratio gives an absolute age.

Carbon-14 (half-life ~5,730 years) is useful for dating organic material up to roughly 50,000 years; older/inorganic materials require systems like uranium-lead or potassium-argon (millions to billions of years), so dinosaur bones (~66 My) cannot be carbon-dated.
learnerActions: Given a parent:daughter ratio and a half-life, set or write the number of half-lives and the approximate age (e.g. one quarter of parent left and a 1.3-billion-year half-life → two half-lives → ~2.6 billion years).

Answer which isotope system would date a stated material: e.g. which clock for a 100-million-year igneous rock (uranium-lead or potassium-argon), and which for a few-thousand-year-old piece of wood or bone (carbon-14).
Order a set of samples from youngest to oldest from their parent:daughter ratios (more daughter relative to parent = older, for the same isotope).
activities.intendedInsight: Once the decay model is understood, the parent:daughter ratio and half-life give a calculable age, and the appropriate isotope depends on both the material and the timescale.

activities.title: Read the decay curve
feedback: If a learner expects a straight line to zero, contrast the halving steps 50% → 25% → 12.5% with a constant-rate (linear) decline.
Confirm that at 25% remaining, two half-lives have passed, not one.
activities.rationale: A fixed annotated curve makes the exponential pattern and its key fractions explicit and is a useful reference; it does not let learners manipulate time or solve inverse problems, so it supports rather than replaces the interactive model.
sourceClaims: Half-life is the time for half of a radioactive parent isotope to decay to its daughter product; measuring the parent:daughter ratio gives an absolute age.
learnerActions: Examine an annotated exponential half-life decay curve and reveal the marked points at 50% (one half-life), 25% (two), and 12.5% (three).
At each point, state the elapsed number of half-lives and the fraction of parent remaining.
Describe in words why the curve flattens and never reaches exactly zero.
activities.intendedInsight: The decay pattern is exponential: equal time intervals each remove half of what remains, so the fraction keeps halving rather than falling linearly to zero.

activities.title: Ask the geochronologist: why not carbon-date a T. rex?
feedback: If a learner thinks the bone itself is dated, clarify that the surrounding volcanic rock is usually dated to bracket the fossil's age.
Reinforce that matching clock to timescale, not the age of the object alone, drives method choice.
activities.rationale: A dialogue format can surface and correct the 'date the fossil itself' and 'carbon dates anything old' misconceptions through explanation; because the underlying relationship is quantitative, this works best as a companion to hands-on model manipulation.
sourceClaims: Carbon-14 (half-life ~5,730 years) is useful for dating organic material up to roughly 50,000 years; older/inorganic materials require systems like uranium-lead or potassium-argon (millions to billions of years), so dinosaur bones (~66 My) cannot be carbon-dated.
learnerActions: Pose the question 'Why can't you carbon-date a dinosaur bone?' and read or discuss the explanation.
Explore the follow-up: why scientists usually date volcanic ash layers above and below a fossil rather than the fossil itself.
Summarise in their own words what is actually being dated and why the choice of isotope matters.
activities.intendedInsight: Carbon-14's ~50,000-year range is far too short for 66-million-year fossils, and fossils are typically dated by bracketing igneous/ash layers whose minerals suit long-lived isotope systems.

constraints: Build exponential intuition by repeated halving of a visible population before introducing the (1/2)^n formula.
Frame dating as reading a ratio of how far decay has run, not a stopwatch started at a known moment.

Half-life (the decay constant) is essentially constant under normal conditions, which is what makes it a reliable clock; the rate of decay itself is not constant but falls exponentially as the parent is depleted — do not describe the process as a 'constant-rate decay'.
Make clear that after two half-lives a quarter of the parent remains; decay is exponential and never cleanly reaches zero.
Clarify that fossils are usually dated via bracketing igneous/volcanic layers, not the fossil itself.

A static decay curve conveys the pattern and key fractions but does not allow manipulating time or solving ratio-to-age problems; pair it with an interactive or computation task when those skills are the goal.
Selection/computation items test maths and clock-choice but do not by themselves build the decay intuition.

A live decay simulation uses stochastic flipping of many atoms to approximate halving; with small grids the result is only approximately half, so note this is a probabilistic model of large populations.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Both listed sources are marked verified:false in the row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original framed carbon-14 as 'useful up to roughly 50,000 years'; this is retained as an approximate upper practical range. Exact limits vary by technique and sample, so treat the figure as indicative.

The original artefact-fit notes asserted a 3D treatment 'adds nothing' and that understanding 'forms' only through manipulation; these comparative-necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been softened to affordance-based statements (static and dialogue formats support specific sub-goals).

Worked numbers added for clarity (1:3 ratio → two half-lives → one quarter parent remaining; 1.3-billion-year half-life → ~2.6 billion years) follow directly from (1/2)^n; verify example half-life values if specific isotopes are used in authoring.

Editor fix (prior pass): activity 1's intendedInsight originally called the process a 'constant-rate decay', which conflicted with the linear/'constant-rate decline' model shown as incorrect in the decay-curve activity; it now refers to a constant half-life with an explicit note that the decay rate itself is not constant.

Editor fix (this pass): the summary previously said the parent 'decays to a daughter at a known rate (half-life)'; reworded to 'with a characteristic, constant half-life' for consistency with the corrected insight and the no-constant-rate constraint. Only the half-life / per-atom decay probability is constant; the aggregate decay rate falls as the parent depletes.

probeDeeper: Why can't we get an absolute age just from which rock layer a fossil sits in?
If a sample has one-quarter of its parent isotope left, how many half-lives have passed?
Why is carbon-14 fine for a 3,000-year-old mummy but useless for a 66-million-year-old dinosaur?
assess.correctAnswer: No. Carbon-14 has a short half-life and is only useful up to roughly 50,000 years, but non-avian dinosaurs are around 66+ million years old — any carbon-14 would have decayed away long ago. Dinosaur-age rock is dated with long-lived isotopes like uranium-lead or potassium-argon. Radiometric dating works by measuring the ratio of parent to daughter isotope: since the parent decays with a known half-life, the ratio gives an absolute age.

errorPatterns.pattern: Carbon dating works on anything old, including dinosaur bones — there's one universal dating method.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce half-life ranges: carbon-14 (~50,000 yr max) versus uranium-lead (millions to billions of years); match the clock to the age.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — carbon dating works on anything old, including dinosaur bones.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Applies carbon-14 to million-year-old material without noticing its time limit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Dating is a stopwatch that started ticking and you just read off elapsed time — not a ratio.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Recast it as a ratio measurement: the proportion of parent left versus daughter formed, read against the known half-life.
errorPatterns.distractor: You just measure how long the clock inside the bone has been ticking.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes dating as counting time directly rather than measuring a parent:daughter ratio.

errorPatterns.pattern: Half-life means the isotope fully decays in that time (or decays at a steady, non-halving rate).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model repeated halving — half remains after one half-life, a quarter after two — not complete or linear decay.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says all the parent is gone after one half-life, or treats decay as linear.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks carbon dating applies to dinosaur bones and treats dating as one universal method.
responseLevels.full: Defines half-life as repeated halving, explains age comes from the parent:daughter ratio, and matches the isotope to the timescale — carbon-14 for recent organics, uranium-lead for dinosaur-age rock.
responseLevels.partial: Knows dinosaurs are too old for carbon-14 OR can define half-life, but can't connect isotope choice to timescale or explain the parent:daughter ratio.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A friend says: 'We can find out how old a dinosaur bone is by carbon-dating it, the same way we date ancient wood or mummies.' Is that right? Explain what radiometric dating measures and why the method matters here.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks all dating is 'carbon dating' with one universal clock says yes. A child who understands half-life and isotope choice explains carbon-14's ~50,000-year limit and picks a long-lived isotope for deep time.
